Appendix A

Systems of ODEs

Many of the equations that appear in these notes can be written naturally as a coupled system of first-order ordinary differential equations. This formulation is especially useful because it provides a unified way of treating several evolving quantities at once, for example, photon propagation, and optical-depth absorption along a sightline.

A generic system of first-order ODEs can be written as \[ \vec{y}'(t,\vec{\theta}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1'(t;\vec{\theta})\\ \vdots\\ y_N'(t;\vec{\theta}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1\bigl(t; y_1(t;\vec{\theta}),\dots,y_N(t;\vec{\theta});\vec{\theta}\bigr)\\[2pt] \vdots\\ f_N\bigl(t; y_1(t;\vec{\theta}),\dots,y_N(t;\vec{\theta});\vec{\theta}\bigr) \end{bmatrix} = \vec{F}\bigl(t,\vec{y}(t;\vec{\theta});\vec{\theta}\bigr). \]

with \[ \vec{y}(t=t_0,\vec{\theta}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1(t=t_0;\vec{\theta}) = y_{1,0}\\ \vdots\\ y_N(t=t_0;\vec{\theta}) = y_{N,0} \end{bmatrix} = \vec{y}_0 \]

This notation is intentionally general. The variable \(t\) plays the role of the independent variable, the vector \(\vec{y}\) collects all unknown functions to be solved for, and \(\vec{\theta}\) denotes any fixed parameters on which the system may depend. Writing the problem in this compact vector form is helpful because many physically different situations reduce to the same mathematical structure once the state vector and the right-hand side \(\vec{F}\) have been specified.

This formulation is also the natural starting point for numerical integration. Once a problem has been cast as a first-order system with an initial condition \(\vec{y}_0\), it can be evolved using standard numerical methods such as Runge–Kutta schemes or other ODE solvers.
